meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A liberal is a man too broadminded to take his own side in a quarrel'?
meta.ogDescription: Frost wrote it as verse in 1941. The polished prose sentence has no Frost source and surfaces in print in 1966, three years after he died.

answer.label: Not in these words — a later paraphrase
answer.authorDates: 1874–1963 · American poet, four Pulitzer Prizes for Poetry
answer.sourceLine: Frost really did make this joke, but he made it in verse: in “The Lesson for Today,” read at Harvard on 20 June 1941 and collected in A Witness Tree (1942), his speaker calls himself liberal and explains that he is so altruistically moral he never takes his own side in a quarrel. The polished prose sentence people quote — with “too broadminded” — is documented nowhere in Frost; the earliest citation in Barry Popik’s chronology is the Chicago Tribune of 30 November 1966, after Frost’s death in January 1963.

I mean so altruistically moral

trail: Frost read “The Lesson for Today” before Harvard’s Phi Beta Kappa Society on 20 June 1941; the poem’s speaker calls himself liberal and says he is so altruistically moral he never takes his own side in a quarrel (poem text and reading date ↗).

Wikiquote carries the popular wording in the chronological 1960s part of its Frost page, citing Harvey Shapiro’s “Story of the Poem” in The New York Times of 15 January 1961 and Guy Davenport’s The Geography of the Imagination (1981), and noting an earlier unattributed version in William Ernest Hocking’s What Man Can Make of Man (1942) (Wikiquote: Robert Frost ↗).

Barry Popik transcribes that same January 1961 column and the January 1962 St. Petersburg Times report with different wordings, and dates the exact “too broad-minded” sentence to the Chicago Tribune of 30 November 1966 (The Big Apple, 6 December 2009 ↗).
Frost died on 29 January 1963 — before the familiar wording appears anywhere in that record (Robert Frost, Wikipedia ↗).
source.excerptNote: Two lines from “The Lesson for Today,” in which Frost’s speaker — a modern poet sparring with a medieval one — calls himself a liberal and then defines the word against himself. Only the couplet is quoted here: the poem is still in copyright.

author.name: Robert Frost
author.heading: Who Robert Frost was
author.metaLine: 1874–1963 · American poet; four Pulitzer Prizes for Poetry
author.bio: Born in San Francisco on 26 March 1874 and long identified with rural New England, Robert Frost became the most publicly recognised American poet of his century, winning the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry four times. He was a far more argumentative and politically sceptical writer than his plain-spoken reputation suggests — A Witness Tree (1942), which carried his fourth Pulitzer, includes the sparring, self-mocking poem this quip comes from. At eighty-six he stood at John F. Kennedy’s inauguration on 20 January 1961, unable to read the new poem he had written in the glare and reciting “The Gift Outright” from memory instead.

misattribution.heading: Right name, wrong sentence
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabricated Frost quote — it is a rewritten one. The joke is genuinely his; the sentence is not.

items.why: Every wording actually recorded from Frost is different. His verse line has him so altruistically moral he never takes his own side in a quarrel; Popik’s January 1961 and January 1962 newspaper citations give “a person who can’t take his own side in a quarrel” and “an extreme liberal is a man who can’t take his own side in a quarrel.” None of them contains “too broadminded” (citation trail ↗).

Wikiquote’s talk page lists the exact popular wording among unsourced Frost quotations with the note that it is “Sometimes attributed to Barry Goldwater” — a second credit with no documentation behind it either (Wikiquote talk page ↗).

Hocking’s What Man Can Make of Man (1942) quotes the taunt as something already in circulation rather than as anyone’s line, which is why researchers describe the origin as uncertain instead of crediting Frost with inventing it. Hocking’s book appeared the year after Frost’s Harvard reading, so it neither confirms nor rules out Frost (Wikiquote’s note ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Frost made the joke — in verse, at Harvard, in June 1941. The smooth prose sentence pinned to him online has never been traced to anything he wrote or said, and its earliest recorded appearance comes years after he died (Barry Popik, The Big Apple ↗).

context.heading: Why the poem matters more than the quip
lead: On 20 June 1941 Frost read “The Lesson for Today” before the Phi Beta Kappa Society at Harvard University. It is a mock-quarrel in rhymed couplets between a modern poet and a medieval one, and in the middle of it Frost’s speaker turns the joke on himself: he calls himself liberal, tells the aristocrat he is arguing with that the word will not mean what he expects, and then defines it as being so altruistically moral that he never takes his own side in a quarrel. The poem went into A Witness Tree the following year, the collection that brought Frost his fourth Pulitzer Prize (poem text and reading date ↗).

Frost kept using the gag in conversation for the rest of his life. Barry Popik’s chronology records him deploying it in January 1961 while talking about John F. Kennedy — whom Frost felt was not that kind of liberal — and again in January 1962. The January 1961 citation is Harvey Shapiro’s column in The New York Times of the 15th, five days before Frost stood at Kennedy’s inauguration; Popik transcribes the wording there as a liberal being a person who can’t take his own side in a quarrel (The Big Apple chronology ↗).
context.detailsSummary: The wrinkle that keeps the origin open
detailsBody: Even Frost’s claim to have invented the gibe is not settled. The philosopher William Ernest Hocking’s What Man Can Make of Man (1942) refers to it as an existing taunt — that a man may be so very liberal he cannot bring himself to take his own side in a quarrel — without crediting anyone, which is why Popik and Wikiquote both stop short of naming Frost as the originator. Hocking’s book appeared the year after Frost’s Harvard reading, so it does not settle the question in either direction (Wikiquote’s note on Hocking ↗).

The wording drifted steadily. Popik’s citations run from “a person who can’t take his own side in a quarrel” in 1961, through “someone who can’t take his own side in an argument” and “an extreme liberal is a man who can’t take his own side in a quarrel,” to the tighter “too broad-minded” construction in 1966 and a blunter “won’t take his own side in a fight” by the late 1980s. What circulates today is the most quotable link in that chain, not the first.
context.pull: Frost made the joke. He just never made it in these words.

sourcesVerified.claim: Barry Popik's entry, dated 6 December 2009, says the saying is usually credited to Robert Frost (1874-1963), that Frost employed it in January 1961 when discussing JFK and again in January 1962, that William Ernest Hocking's What Man Can Make of Man (1942) contains similar language quoted as a 'gibe', and that the origin is uncertain. Its chronology lists the New York Times, 15 January 1961 ('A liberal is a person who can't take his own side in a quarrel'), the St. Petersburg Times, 24 January 1962 ('An extreme liberal is a man who can't take his own side in a quarrel'), and the Chicago Tribune, 30 November 1966 ('A liberal is a man too broad-minded to take his own side in a quarrel').

Wikiquote's Robert Frost page lists 'A liberal is a man too broadminded to take his own side in a quarrel' in the chronological 1960s section, with the note 'Attributed to Frost in Harvey Shapiro "Story of the Poem", The New York Times (January 15, 1961), sec. SM, p. 6; and in Guy Davenport, The Geography of the Imagination (San Francisco: North Point Press, 1981), p. 208. An earlier unattributed version of this quip appeared in William Ernest Hocking, What Man Can Make of Man (1942)...'. The same page cites 'The Lesson for Today' under its 'A Witness Tree (1942)' section.

This page reproduces the lines 'I'm liberal. You, you aristocrat, / Won't know exactly what I mean by that. / I mean so altruistically moral / I never take my own side in a quarrel.' from Robert Frost's 'The Lesson for Today', and states the poem was presented at Harvard's Phi Beta Kappa Society on 20 June 1941.

This page reproduces 'I mean so altruistically moral / I never take my own side in a quarrel.' from 'The Lesson for Today' and states the poem was read before the Phi Beta Kappa Society at Harvard University on 20 June 1941, with the text retyped from Selected Poems of Robert Frost (1963 edition).
A Witness Tree was first published in 1942 by Henry Holt and Company and won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1943.

Robert Frost was born 26 March 1874 in San Francisco and died 29 January 1963 in Boston; he won four Pulitzer Prizes for Poetry (1924, 1931, 1937, 1943); at age 86 he took part in John F. Kennedy's inaugural ceremony on 20 January 1961, reciting 'The Gift Outright' from memory after sunlight prevented him reading his new poem.
The Internet Archive holds a scan of Robert Frost's 'A witness tree', published by H. Holt and Company in 1942, and access to it is restricted (lending-limited).
